I am 75 years old. I have worked this same 6 mu in Quzhou County for 50 years, and I know every ridge and furrow. My wife and I still do the daily work, though our sons and daughters-in-law have factory jobs in town and only come back to help at harvest. We have a well, so when the rain does not come, I can still water the crops—but I do not waste a drop.

I split the land the way I always have: 4 mu for the wheat-maize rotation, and 2 mu for cotton. The wheat and maize keep grain in the house and give a steady harvest twice a year from the same patch. Cotton is more work and more risk, but when the price is right, it brings in more cash than grain.

For the winter wheat, I sow an improved variety in early October. I trust the old reliable seeds; they do not surprise me. Before sowing, I spread base fertilizer and then topdress nitrogen in spring when the wheat turns green. I irrigate three times from the well: once before winter to protect the seedlings from the cold, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once at heading to fill the grain. I use the rotary tiller; at my age, it is easier on my back than the old plough. Two sprays are enough—one for weeds after sowing, and one for rust or insects if the weather turns wet.

For summer maize, I plant hybrid seed immediately after cutting the wheat in early June. Hybrid maize grows fast and strong in the heat. I put down fertilizer at sowing and side-dress more nitrogen when the plants are knee-high. Two irrigations are enough if the summer rains cooperate: one at tasseling and one at grain-filling. Rotary tillage is all I need because the wheat stubble is already broken up.

For cotton, I plough deep in spring. Cotton roots need loose, deep soil, so I do not skip the plough. I plant an improved variety. Cotton needs more potassium than grain crops, so I give it extra potash. I irrigate three times during flowering and boll-setting, and I spray four times—you cannot skip sprays on cotton, or the bollworms will ruin everything in a week.

I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat, 600 kg per mu from the maize if the autumn rains are kind, and around 280 kg per mu of seed cotton. These are honest yields for honest work, and at my age, I do not chase miracles. I just farm the land the way it has always been farmed.
